--- title: "Introduction to Quarto — Lab" subtitle: "RaukR 2026 · Day 1" author: "" date: "" format: html: toc-location: left # free the right margin for the "Quarto docs" pointers --- ::: {.callout-note} ## Scope Build one penguins document with the authoring extras, then **cite it** and render it as a **branded Typst PDF**. You will use one document for two challenges, with a break between them. The result follows the same path from an analysis to a submission-ready report. Everything runs on **base-R `datasets::penguins`** (R ≥ 4.5), so there is no data to download. **Before you start:** work through the **[Setup page](../../setup.qmd)** if you haven't. Its `00-check-setup.R` confirms R, Quarto, and the packages this lab uses. ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} You are working in the **`day1-intro/`** folder from the exercises download (open `day1-intro.Rproj`). See the [Setup page](../../setup.qmd#get-the-materials). Everything you render is written next to your files. You start from a file that is already there, `authoring-starter.qmd`, and the other files are used later, each at the step that names it (the folder's README lists them). ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Coming from R Markdown? (optional) You do **not** need to convert anything to work natively in Quarto. Start with `.qmd` directly. But if you have an `.Rmd` you want to bring over: - it renders **as-is** (Quarto reads `.Rmd` too). - cell options move from the chunk header to the `#|` "hash-pipe" (one YAML option per line). - `knitr::convert_chunk_header("doc.Rmd", output = "doc.qmd")` does the mechanical part. The rest of this lab uses native `.qmd`. ::: ## Authoring Challenge > **Goal:** a penguins report with a cross-referenced **figure**, a cross-referenced **table**, and a > **margin** element, rendered to HTML. **Starting point.** Open **`day1-intro/authoring-starter.qmd`** and save it as **`my-report.qmd`**, in that same folder (next to `references.bib` / `apa.csl` / `_brand.yml`, so Part 2's paths and branding resolve later). Render it once to confirm it works, then re-render after every step below. The starter is already a working report, but it has no numbering, captions, cross-references, or alt text. Most steps require no R changes. The accessibility step makes two small changes to the plot. ::: {.column-margin} {{< fa book-open >}} **Quarto docs** [Cross-references](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html) · [Article layout](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/article-layout.html) · [Accessibility](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-accessibility.html) ::: Missing the download? Take the source directly: {{< fa download >}} authoring-starter.qmd ### Cross-reference the figure **Goal.** Turn the scatter plot into a **numbered figure with a caption**, and refer to that number from the prose. Two edits: an option on the **cell**, and a reference in the **body text** above it. Docs: [Cross-references](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html). ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false} ## {{< fa circle-check >}} You should see A caption **Figure 1: …** under the plot, and the sentence above it opening with a live **Figure 1** link. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Which cell options tell Quarto to number this figure, and how do you refer to it in the text? A cell becomes cross-referenceable when its label starts with a known prefix (`fig-` for a figure) and is unique in the document. The caption is a second cell option. Label, caption and the `@fig-something` reference work together: a reference with no matching label renders as `?@fig-something`. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution On the plot cell: ```r #| label: fig-bill #| fig-cap: "Bill length versus depth, colored by species." ``` And the sentence above the cell, rewritten to point at it: ``` markdown @fig-bill shows that within a species the bill has a characteristic shape, so the species form clusters. ``` ::: ### Cross-reference the table **Goal.** Apply the same method to the summary table under **Mean measurements**: a numbered, captioned **Table 1**, introduced by a sentence that links to it. The `gt` call is already written. Docs: [Cross-references for tables](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html#tables). ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false} ## {{< fa circle-check >}} You should see **Table 1: …** above the table (table captions go above, figure captions below), and a sentence introducing it with a live **Table 1** link. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Figures and tables are numbered in separate sequences. Which label prefix tells Quarto this one is a table? Use `#| label: tbl-summary` and `#| tbl-cap:` on the cell, then `@tbl-summary` in the prose. The prefix decides both the sequence and the word ("Figure", "Table") Quarto prints. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution On the `gt` cell: ```r #| label: tbl-summary #| tbl-cap: "Mean measurements per species." ``` And above it: ``` markdown @tbl-summary reports the mean bill measurements and body mass per species. ``` ::: ### Move the counts into the margin **Goal.** Put the species-counts table in the **right margin**, beside the paragraph that mentions it, instead of in the main text column. Docs: [Article layout](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/article-layout.html). ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false} ## {{< fa circle-check >}} You should see The counts table in the right-hand margin, level with "The species are not evenly represented:", and the main text column unchanged in width. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint The R code does not change. Where do you tell Quarto that its output belongs elsewhere on the page? Add `#| column: margin` to the cell. That option also takes `body`, `body-outset`, `page` and `screen`. For prose rather than cell output, use a `::: {.column-margin}` div. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution On the counts cell: ```r #| column: margin ``` ::: ### Make the figure accessible **Goal.** Make the figure readable by someone who cannot distinguish the colors, and by someone using a screen reader. The plot separates species by **color alone**, in ggplot2's default palette, which is not color-blind-safe. This is the one step that edits the R: two changes to the plot, one option on the cell. `ggokabeito` is already loaded in the setup cell. Docs: [HTML accessibility](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-accessibility.html) · [Figure alt text](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/figures.html#alt-text). ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false} ## {{< fa circle-check >}} You should see Each species drawn with **its own shape as well as its own color**, in the Okabe-Ito palette (orange, blue, green rather than ggplot2's salmon, green and blue), and one legend for both color and shape. The alt text is not visible on the page: to check it, view the page source and confirm the `` tag carries your `alt="…"`. The finished figure looks like this: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Target: bill length versus depth by species.](index_files/figure-html/fig-target-1.png){#fig-target fig-alt='Scatter plot of bill depth against bill length for three penguin species in distinct colors. The species form largely separate clusters.' width=576} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Someone who cannot separate the three colors needs a second way to tell the species apart. What else can `aes()` map? Where does the plot description go when the other figure settings are cell options? Map `shape = species` alongside `color = species` in `aes()`, and add `scale_color_okabe_ito()`. The description is the cell option `#| fig-alt:`. It is not the caption: the alt text stands in for the image, so it describes what the plot *shows*, not what it *is*. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution On the plot cell, next to the label and caption: ```r #| fig-alt: >- #| Scatter plot of bill depth against bill length for penguins of three species, each drawn in a #| distinct color and shape. The three species form largely separate clusters. ``` And in the plot itself: ```r ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_len, bill_dep, color = species, shape = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.8) + scale_color_okabe_ito() + labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)", color = "Species", shape = "Species") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` Naming both `color` and `shape` in `labs()` merges them into a single legend. ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ## {{< fa universal-access >}} Optional accessibility check Your figure now has alt text and redundant color/shape encoding. To check the whole page: - add `axe: {output: document}` under `format: html`, re-preview, and a WCAG report appears on the page (drop it again before you publish). See [Quarto's accessibility docs](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-accessibility.html). ::: ### Add a numbered equation *(stretch)* **Goal.** Add the bill-shape ratio (bill length divided by bill depth) as a **numbered display equation**, and refer to it from the prose. One caution: inside `$$…$$`, `bill_len` can render as a subscript, so escape the underscore as `bill\_len`. Docs: [Equations](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html#equations). ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false} ## {{< fa circle-check >}} You should see The formula centered on its own line with **(1)** at the right margin, and the sentence above it linking to that number. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Display math is not a cell, so the label cannot be a cell option. Where can you attach it? The label is an attribute on the closing `$$`, written `{#eq-ratio}`. The `eq-` prefix makes it a numbered equation, and `@eq-ratio` links to it like `@fig-` and `@tbl-`. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution ``` markdown A compact descriptor of bill shape is the length-to-depth ratio (@eq-ratio): $$ \text{ratio} = \frac{\text{bill\_len}}{\text{bill\_dep}} $$ {#eq-ratio} ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false} ## {{< fa circle-check >}} Checkpoint: the whole document A numbered **Figure 1** (the bill scatter, three separate clusters), a numbered **Table 1**, and the counts in the right margin. `@fig-bill` and `@tbl-summary` render as live links, with no `?@` markers anywhere. If you did the stretch step, you also have a numbered **Equation 1**. ::: **`authoring-checkpoint.qmd` is this same report with every step above applied.** It is already in `day1-intro/`. Compare your work against it, or, if you did not finish, save a copy of it as `my-report.qmd` and continue into Part 2 from there. You can also take the source: {{< fa download >}} authoring-checkpoint.qmd ## Citations Challenge > **Goal:** cite the report, then render the *same document* as a **branded Typst PDF**. ::: {.callout-note} ## Starting point If you finished the Authoring Challenge, continue in **`my-report.qmd`**. Otherwise: 1. Open **`day1-intro/authoring-checkpoint.qmd`** (the completed Part-1 report). 2. Save a copy as **`my-report.qmd`** in `day1-intro/`, next to `references.bib`, `apa.csl`, and `_brand.yml`. 3. Continue in that copy. The instructions below use `my-report.qmd` for both routes. ::: :::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## {{< fa clipboard-list >}} Tasks ::: {.column-margin} {{< fa book-open >}} **Quarto docs** [Citations](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/citations.html) · [Typst](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html) · [Brand](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/brand.html) ::: 1. Point the document header at the shared bibliography and citation style: ```yaml bibliography: references.bib csl: apa.csl ``` 2. Cite the two sources the opening paragraph already credits, without rewriting it. The sentence ending *"…collected at Palmer Station, Antarctica."* takes the data citation before the period (`Antarctica [@gorman2014].`), and the sentence crediting the **palmerpenguins** package takes `[@horst2020]` the same way. Don't paste a second copy of either sentence. 3. Add a **References** section where the list should appear: ```markdown ## References {.unnumbered} ::: {#refs} ::: ``` 4. Give it a real **title block** so the PDF reads as a paper. **Replace** your document's `author:` line (or add one) with: ```yaml author: - name: Your Name affiliation: Your Lab, Your University ``` 5. Render to HTML and confirm that both citations resolve as *(Gorman et al., 2014)* and *(Horst et al., 2020)*, with a reference list holding both entries. 6. Switch the output to **Typst** and render a branded PDF. The branding comes from `_brand.yml`, which Quarto reads next to the document you render, so keep `my-report.qmd` in `day1-intro/`. You may see `unknown font family` warnings on the first render. See Troubleshooting if the final PDF still uses a serif font. Two routes: - **CLI** — leave the header as-is and force the target: ```bash quarto render my-report.qmd --to typst ``` - **Editor Render button** — set `format: typst` in the YAML header first, *then* click Render. The button renders whatever `format:` is declared, so while the header still says `format: html` the button gives you HTML, **not** a PDF. The PDF is written **next to its source** in `day1-intro/`. :::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false} ## {{< fa circle-check >}} You should see In-text **(Gorman et al., 2014)** and **(Horst et al., 2020)**, a **References** section formatted in APA with both entries, and, in the Typst PDF, the same citations and reference list, typeset with the RaukR palette. No `?@gorman2014`, `?@horst2020` or `[?]` markers anywhere. **Check the branding applied.** An unbranded PDF builds without any error, so check the font instead: a branded PDF is set in **Albert Sans**, an unbranded one in Typst's default serif. Serif headings mean `_brand.yml` isn't next to your `.qmd` (see Troubleshooting). ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint - The `@key` in `[@gorman2014]` must match a key in `references.bib` **exactly**. - `csl:` sets the style (here APA). Swap the file to restyle every citation at once. - Typst reads the `.bib` itself, so keep bibliography fields plain (avoid LaTeX macros like `\emph{}` in titles). - The first Typst render requires a network connection while Quarto downloads the brand's Google fonts. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution: the header and citations In the YAML header: ``` yaml bibliography: references.bib csl: apa.csl ``` In the prose, append each citation to the sentence that credits its source: ``` markdown … collected at Palmer Station, Antarctica [@gorman2014]. The data are available through the **palmerpenguins** package [@horst2020] and are now also included in base R's `datasets` package. ``` A References section (the list renders inside the `#refs` div): ``` markdown ## References {.unnumbered} ::: {#refs} ::: ``` For the branded PDF (`day1-intro/_brand.yml` styles it), either force the target from the CLI: ``` bash quarto render my-report.qmd --to typst ``` or set `format: typst` in the header and use the editor's Render button. :::: **`solutions/day1/penguins-report.qmd` is the complete Day-1 report:** the starter with every step of both challenges applied. Try the challenge first, then open it to compare, or take the source: {{< fa download >}} penguins-report.qmd For a more advanced branded PDF example, render `day1-intro/sample-typst.qmd`. It also styles its table and plot in R and sets Typst page options. Those additions are outside this exercise. ## Bonus — one report per species (optional) {#sec-parameters} > **Goal:** turn a report into a *parameterized* one: a single source that renders a **separate > report per species** by passing the species at render time. This section is optional. Skip it if > time is short. A **parameter** is a value declared in the YAML that your code can read as `params$…`. Change the value at render time and the *same document* produces a different report. You do not need separate source files. ::: {.callout-note} ## Starting point Open **`day1-intro/parameters-starter.qmd`**. It contains the report structure, data, and plot. Your task is to make the species an input to the document. A complete reference is available at **`solutions/day1/penguins-by-species.qmd`**. ::: :::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## {{< fa clipboard-list >}} Tasks ::: {.column-margin} {{< fa book-open >}} **Quarto docs** [Parameters](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/parameters.html) ::: 1. Declare a parameter with a default in the header: ```yaml params: species: Gentoo ``` 2. **Use it to filter** in the setup cell. `params$species` is a value. Keep the existing missing-value checks and add the species condition: ```r one <- penguins |> filter(species == params$species, !is.na(bill_len), !is.na(bill_dep)) ``` 3. **Use the parameter in the report.** Three places, marked `TODO 3a`, `3b` and `3c` in the file. Replace the placeholder species in the opening sentence with inline code (`` `{{r}} params$species` ``), and name the species in the closing sentence the same way. Make the caption and alt text track the parameter with `!expr`. Cell options are YAML, so the `!expr` tag tells Quarto to evaluate the R expression: ```yaml #| fig-cap: !expr paste0("Bill length versus depth for ", params$species, " penguins.") #| fig-alt: !expr paste0("Scatter plot of bill depth against bill length for ", params$species, " penguins.") ``` 4. **Render a different species from the CLI** with `-P name:value`. Run this from inside `day1-intro/`: ```bash quarto render parameters-starter.qmd -P species:Adelie ``` With no `-P`, the default (`Gentoo`) is used. :::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Stretch: dynamic headings and standalone files Replace the static `## Species at a glance` heading with a cell that emits Markdown: ````markdown ```{{r}} #| echo: false #| output: asis cat("##", params$species, "at a glance\n") ``` ```` To keep two named reports, render each as a self-contained HTML file: ```bash quarto render parameters-starter.qmd -P species:Adelie --output adelie.html --embed-resources quarto render parameters-starter.qmd -P species:Chinstrap --output chinstrap.html --embed-resources ``` `--output` prevents the second render from overwriting the first. `--embed-resources` puts each plot inside its HTML file, so the reports do not share a figure-support folder. ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false} ## {{< fa circle-check >}} You should see Rendering with `-P species:Adelie` gives a report whose sentences, figure caption, alt text, point count, and plot are all about Adelie. Nothing says Gentoo. Rendering without `-P` produces the Gentoo report. If you completed the stretch task, the heading also names the selected species. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint - Parameters **must have defaults**: `params$species` has to resolve when no `-P` is passed. - `-P` takes `name:value` (`-P species:Adelie`). Pass several with repeated `-P` flags. - The plot must use the filtered object `one`, not the full `penguins` data. ::: **The complete, runnable solution is `solutions/day1/penguins-by-species.qmd`.** Open it to compare your work or render it with different `-P species:` values. You can also take the source: {{< fa download >}} penguins-by-species.qmd ## Troubleshooting ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon=false} ## {{< fa wrench >}} If rendering fails or the output looks wrong - **YAML is indentation-sensitive.** If rendering fails *before* any code runs, check the YAML header for stray spaces, tabs, or unmatched quotes. - **Missing package?** `install.packages("")` (or `renv::restore()`) and render again. - **A figure doesn't appear?** Check the path is relative to the `.qmd` and the filename matches exactly (case included). - **A cross-reference shows `?@…`?** The cell label must start with `fig-`/`tbl-`/`eq-` and be unique, and the `@ref` must match it. - **A citation shows `?@gorman2014` or `[?]`?** The `@key` doesn't match a key in `references.bib`, or `bibliography:` isn't set. - **`references.bib` not found, although the download has it?** Your `.qmd` is probably not in `day1-intro/` (saved to the top folder, for example). Move it next to `references.bib` / `apa.csl` / `_brand.yml` and render again. - **Do I need to install Typst?** No. Typst is bundled in Quarto ≥ 1.9, so there's nothing extra to install (no LaTeX either). Check `quarto --version`. - **Typst PDF looks unbranded / wrong fonts?** An unbranded render succeeds silently, so check the font, not the log: branded is **Albert Sans**, unbranded is Typst's default serif. Confirm `_brand.yml` is in your `day1-intro/` folder (next to the `.qmd`) and you have network on the first render (Quarto fetches the Google fonts once). Missing the file? Download [`_brand.yml`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cderv/raukr-2026-quarto-exercises/main/day1-intro/_brand.yml) into the folder holding your `.qmd`. - **Typst prints `unknown font family` warnings?** Harmless: a `gt` table names a generic `sans-serif` in its font stack, and Typst doesn't recognize that as a family. The PDF still builds, branding included. - **Prefer to stay in HTML first?** Render HTML, get it right, *then* switch to `format: typst`. The content is the same. ::: ## Session {.appendix .unnumbered}
